items.title: Jerry Blumberg Interview, 1961-04-15
items.q: The interviewer mentions George Mitchell as an example of a trumpet player with a characteristic sound; the interviewee responds by discussing trumpet players generally without confirming a personal interaction or specific relationship with Mitchell.

ctx.x: Yeah, it was fast. It was fast.

The general sound of his horn is always fascinating me. I've always wanted to know how he got it. You know, because it's, it's a very characteristic sound. Yeah. Like, uh, Bonk's, or George Mitchell's, his characteristic, you know.

Well, I would say of the trumpet players I've heard down here, uh, as far as the approach to the horn, the horn is a little bit more than the horn is a little bit more than the horn is a little bit more than the horn.

items.title: Jerry Blumberg Interview, 1961-04-06
items.q: I remember there was one time when Bunker staying at Loft was up later that they got to playing him some jelly roll records and he became very enamored of George Mitchell's playing which he had apparently he had never been aware of how fine Mitchell was

ctx.x: You were talking about vibrato, you were talking about his...

Yeah, well, I was very interested to see. Vibrato is a funny thing. It's... On records, fast vibrato doesn't usually sound very good. I've noticed Sidney Vachey's vibrato on records doesn't have the same effect that it has in person. Yeah, but in person, when you can hear this full rich tone, the vibrato just seems to enhance it completely and you don't get any of the unpleasant illusions that you get on a record. And the same thing is true of Bunk's vibrato. In person, it was just the most beautiful sound. Yeah,…
Yeah, Jimmy Noon. I haven't heard that for so many years, I don't remember what it's like.
